UNOROUTER_VS_RISUAI.INTRO: RisuAI is one of the best character chat frontends out there, and we studied its source closely. UNOROUTER_VS_RISUAI.P_ENGINE: The parts that make Risu great are in {appName} because we ported them: the single-pool lorebook with @@decorators (depth, role, probability, priority, recursion, inject-lore) and a token budget, the CBS macro language with around 170 macros, the V1 and V2 trigger system with Lua, regex customscripts across editinput, editoutput, and editdisplay, SillyTavern card v2 and v3 plus .charx import, group chats, personas, and presets. If you know Risu's lorebooks and triggers, they work the way you expect.
UNOROUTER_VS_RISUAI.H_TWO_IN_ONE: One key for code and chat

The same key that runs the character chat also points Claude Code, Cline, or Codex at 200+ models, and still drops into SillyTavern, Janitor.AI, or Chub if you prefer those. One account, one balance, work and play.
UNOROUTER_VS_RISUAI.P_HOSTING: Risu you run yourself and paste each provider's key. {appName} is hosted: nothing to install, no keys to gather, since the key is the account. You sign up and chat. That removes the whole setup step.

LAUNCH.TITLE: We got tired of fake Claude. So we built {appName}.
LAUNCH.DESCRIPTION: Outages every other week. Premium models silently swapped for cheap clones. We snapped, shipped our own router, and made it paranoid about both. Here is the launch story.
LAUNCH.AUTHOR: {appName} team
LAUNCH.INTRO: The cheap AI API market has two problems. Providers go down a lot, and some of them quietly forward your request to a weaker model while still charging you for the flagship. {appName} is built to fix both.
LAUNCH.P_UPTIME: Cheap upstreams are cheap for a reason. They rate-limit, throttle, and drop connections under load. When one degrades, {appName} routes the same request to another healthy provider serving the same model, automatically. Your application doesn't see the outage. You don't rewrite your code. You just keep shipping.
LAUNCH.H_AUTHENTIC: Every model is the real model
LAUNCH.P_AUTHENTIC: Not every gateway serves what it advertises. Some forward premium model names to cheaper substitutes and hope you don't notice. {appName} validates authenticity on every model we list: we probe identity and behavior end to end, and if a provider lies, we cut them. When you call Claude, you get Claude. When you call GPT, you get GPT.
LAUNCH.H_HARNESS: Works in the terminals you actually use
LAUNCH.P_HARNESS: A model is only useful if it works in your tools. We test every model end to end for HTTP completion, streaming, and tool calling. Those three capabilities are what AI terminal harnesses depend on. If a model is in our catalog, it works in Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and any OpenAI-compatible client. No surprise 'streaming not supported' failures mid-session.
LAUNCH.P_NEXT: We ship weekly. Expect more models, tighter health signals driving smarter fallbacks, richer cost and latency dashboards, and deeper integrations with the terminals and IDEs you already live in.

AGENT_READY.TITLE: We pointed Cloudflare's agent scanner at our site. It came back 100/100.
AGENT_READY.DESCRIPTION: Cloudflare just shipped a scanner that grades how ready your site is for AI agents. We hit a perfect 100/100 and the top Level 5 rating. Here is exactly what it checks and why most sites fail.
AGENT_READY.AUTHOR: {appName} team
AGENT_READY.INTRO: An AI agent walks up to your domain. Can it figure out who you are, what you offer, how to talk to you, and how to pay you? That is the question Cloudflare's Is Your Site Agent-Ready scanner tries to answer. We pointed it at {appDomain} and got back a perfect 100/100 with the top-tier Level 5 Agent-Native rating.
AGENT_READY.P_SCORE: Five categories, all green. Discoverability 3/3, Content 1/1, Bot Access Control 3/3, API/Auth/MCP/Skill Discovery 7/7, and the optional Commerce category passing as well. As far as the scanner is concerned, every emerging agent standard it knows how to look for is in place on {appDomain}.
AGENT_READY.IMG_ALT: Is Your Site Agent-Ready report card showing {appDomain} with a 100 score and Level 5 Agent-Native badge
AGENT_READY.H_WHAT: What Is Your Site Agent-Ready actually checks
AGENT_READY.P_WHAT: It is a free Cloudflare scanner that hits your domain and looks for the technical signals AI agents use to discover and interact with a site. Think of it as a checklist: robots.txt, sitemap, link headers, content-type negotiation for markdown, AI bot rules, MCP server cards, agent skill manifests, OAuth discovery documents, x402 payment headers, and several emerging commerce protocols. Each check is one small HTTP call against a well-known path or header.
AGENT_READY.P_CATEGORIES: Discoverability covers robotsTxt (a robots.txt that parses), sitemap (a sitemap.xml the scanner can fetch), and linkHeaders (Link: headers that point at machine-readable manifests). Content covers markdownNegotiation (whether the site responds with markdown when an agent asks for it). Bot Access Control covers robotsTxtAiRules (explicit AI-agent allow/deny rules), contentSignals (Cloudflare's content-signals format) and webBotAuth (signed bot identity). API/Auth/MCP/Skill Discovery covers apiCatalog (a discoverable API listing), oauthDiscovery and oauthProtectedResource (RFC 9728 OAuth metadata), mcpServerCard (a Model Context Protocol server descriptor), a2aAgentCard (Google's Agent-to-Agent card), agentSkills (declared skill list) and webMcp (HTTP-bound MCP). Commerce covers x402 (the HTTP 402 payment standard), mpp, ucp and acp (three competing autonomous-commerce drafts). {appDomain} answers correctly on all of them.
AGENT_READY.P_STUBS: These checks are simple stubs. The scanner mostly verifies that a well-known URL exists, returns a 200, and contains the right top-level shape. It does not run a real OAuth flow, it does not actually invoke an MCP tool, it does not settle an x402 payment. A green tick means the door is unlocked, not that the room behind it is finished. Anyone who depends on a protocol in production should still do their own end-to-end verification: round-trip the OAuth flow, call the MCP tool from a real client, run an x402 payment all the way to settlement. The score is a great signal that the surface area is in place. It is not a substitute for protocol-level conformance testing.
AGENT_READY.H_TRY: Run it on your own site
AGENT_READY.P_TRY: If you build anything that AI agents might one day touch, the scanner is genuinely worth a minute of your time. It surfaces a long list of small standards in one view and tells you exactly which well-known paths are missing or malformed. We use it as a regression check whenever we ship anything that touches discovery, auth, or commerce surfaces.
AGENT_READY.CTA: Scan your site at <scanner>isitagentready.com</scanner>, or if you came here for {appName}, <register>grab an API key</register> and start routing.

CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.TITLE: Your cheap Claude is probably a fake. We caught 183 of them.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.DESCRIPTION: We probed 8 popular Claude resellers for 17 days. 183 of their channels were not Claude at all. Most were Kiro Cascade or Codeium wearing a Claude name tag. Names, numbers, and the script we used so you can test your own provider.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.AUTHOR: {appName} team
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.H_NOT_SPOOFING: What is not spoofing: Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.H_RESULTS: What 17 days of probing turned up
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.H_TEST: Test your own provider in 5 minutes
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.INTRO_P1: Claude is the most in-demand model on the market right now, and one of the most expensive. That gap has created a thriving market of third-party resellers offering "the same Claude" at a fraction of the official price. Some are legitimate. A lot aren't.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.INTRO_P2: Over 17 days of automated probing across <s>8 upstream resellers</s>, we found <s>183 (channel, model) pairs</s> that fail authenticity checks against models marketed as <c>claude-opus-4-7</c>, <c>claude-sonnet-4-6</c>, <c>claude-haiku-4-5</c>, and friends. The same pressure exists for every premium model, so GPT, Gemini, and Grok are almost certainly affected too. Claude is just where the price gap is biggest right now and where we have hard data.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.PROBES_P: Per (channel, model) we send four parallel requests to the standard Anthropic Messages API (<c>POST /v1/messages</c>):
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.PROBE_EMOTIONAL_PROMPT: Tell me a 2-sentence sad story about a lost kitten.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.PROBE_CREATIVE_PROMPT: Write a haiku about the ocean at sunrise. Only the haiku, nothing else.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.PROBE_IDENTITY_PROMPT: What company created you? Reply with only the company name, one word.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.PROBE_MODELNAME_PROMPT: Which model are you? Reply with only your model name, nothing else.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.FAILURE_CODING: coding-tool-refusal: response matches a Kiro Cascade or Codeium / Windsurf Droid refusal pattern ("I'm here to help with coding", "I'm Droid", etc.). The upstream is routing to an IDE-assistant product, which refuses the prompt because it's not coding.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.FAILURE_FOREIGN: <c>foreign-identity</c>: response identifies as a non-Anthropic vendor (OpenAI, Meta, DeepSeek, Moonshot, etc.).
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.FAILURE_FAILED: <c>failed</c>: wrong-style output without those signals (no kitten story, no haiku, generic "AI assistant" reply).
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.NOT_SPOOFING_P1: A reseller routing through <s>AWS Bedrock</s>, <s>Google Vertex AI</s>, or <s>Azure AI Foundry</s> is not spoofing. Those platforms host real Anthropic Claude weights under license. Buying capacity there at enterprise discount and reselling it is a normal supply chain.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.NOT_SPOOFING_P2: One known false positive: cloud-hosted Claude sometimes answers the identity probe with Amazon / Google / Microsoft instead of Anthropic, because of host system prompts. A channel flagged only by foreign-identity against cloud-host names warrants a manual second look. coding-tool-refusal and non-cloud foreign vendors are unambiguous, real Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry Claude never produces those responses.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.RESULTS_INTRO: 8 upstream resellers (anonymized as <c>provider-1</c>..<c>provider-8</c>), 183 (channel, model) entries between 2026-04-08 and 2026-04-24.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.RESULTS_LABELS_INTRO: <s>Probe labels that triggered failures</s> (a channel can fail multiple):
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.EMOTIONAL_GUN: <s><c>emotional</c> being the biggest catcher is the smoking gun.</s> Real Claude doesn't refuse to write a 2-sentence sad story about a kitten. A coding-tool backend dressed as Claude does, every time.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.OLDER_VARIANTS: Older Claude variants have higher counts only because they've been on the market longer. Opus 4.7 hit 16 spoofed channels within weeks of release. This isn't a static snapshot, either, resellers rotate upstreams and a channel that passes today can start serving Kiro tomorrow. <s>Authenticity has to be checked continuously.</s>
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.WHY_INTRO: Real Claude is expensive whether you buy from Anthropic or from a licensed cloud reseller. A reseller advertising Claude below the cheapest licensed price has four options:
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.WHY_OPT1: Eat the loss (sustainable only with deep funding).
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.WHY_OPT2: Buy Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry capacity at enterprise discount and resell. <s>Legitimate</s>, but bounded by what those clouds charge.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.WHY_OPT3: Run a fraction of traffic through real Claude and route the rest cheaper, banking on users not noticing.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.WHY_OPT4: Route everything to a non-Anthropic backend and hope nobody checks.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.WHY_OUTRO: Options 3 and 4 are what the probes catch. Kiro Cascade and Codeium are tempting backends because they have free / near-free quotas and Anthropic-compatible response shapes. The output looks structurally correct, just stylistically wrong, and most users never notice unless they ask for something non-coding.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.TEST_TESTER: We built these probes into the site so you do not have to run anything. Open the <link>API model tester</link>, paste your provider base URL and key, pick a Claude model, and it runs the same authenticity checks live and shows you exactly which probes failed. Prefer the command line? The raw curl below is the emotional probe.
CLAUDE_AUTHENTICITY.TEST_OUTRO: If the response refuses or redirects to coding, your "Claude" is not Claude. For a second check, send "What company created you? Reply with only the company name, one word." anything other than Anthropic is your answer.

SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.TITLE: Which image models actually take 6 reference inputs? We ran the benchmark.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.DESCRIPTION: Many image models advertise multi-reference editing, but availability across resellers varies wildly. We sent a fixed 6-image scene-composition prompt to every image channel in our catalog. 332 channel runs, 136 unique models, 54 with at least one verified passing provider.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.AUTHOR: {appName} team
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.INTRO_P1: Modern image models can take multiple reference images plus one text prompt and compose them into a single output. <s>One prompt, N references, one composite</s>. Useful for visual novels, brand collateral with consistent characters, product mockups, comic panels, and any workflow that needs a scene assembled from known parts.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.INTRO_P2: The catch: every model in the marketplace claims to do this. Most do not. Some cap at 1 reference, some at 4, some accept the inputs but silently ignore everything past the first. And on top of that the same model behaves differently across resellers because of quotas, slug variants, and missing endpoint wiring. So we ran a benchmark.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.FIXTURES_P: Six fixed JPEGs covering a typical character scene composition: one tavern background and five character portraits (one user-side and four NPCs). Same six files for every (provider, model) pair, no per-channel rewriting. Total payload roughly 500 KB across the six images.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.FIXTURES_PROMPT_INTRO: The text prompt is fixed too. It names each character, references each image by index, and asks for a single composite. Verbatim:
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.METHOD_P1: For every (provider, model) pair in the catalog: POST the six fixtures plus the prompt to that channel's <c>/v1/images/edits</c>. <s>Pass</s> = HTTP 200 with a non-empty image URL or base64 payload in the response. <s>Fail</s> = non-200, empty body, or shape mismatch. No human grading. The benchmark is reproducible, runs on demand, and re-runs whenever a new image model appears upstream.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.METHOD_P2: We do not score visual quality here. This run answers one question only: does the model accept six reference inputs plus a prompt and return an image, on this specific channel, right now? Quality grading is a separate pass.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.RESULTS_INTRO: Across <s>8 upstream resellers</s>, we tested <s>136 unique image models</s> over <s>332 channel runs</s>. <s>54 models</s> have at least one verified passing provider. Run captured <c>2026-05-09</c>.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.RESULTS_FAMILY_INTRO: Grouped by family. <s>Verified models</s> = distinct SKUs in that family with at least one passing channel. <s>Passing-provider sum</s> = total count of (model, provider) pairs that returned 200 across the family.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.RESULTS_TOP_INTRO: <s>Top single-model winners</s> by passing-provider count. More passing providers means better routing headroom: when one upstream rate-limits or goes down, the router has another path to the same model.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.H_GOTCHAS: Why a model passes on one reseller and fails on another
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.GOTCHAS_P1: Three common reasons. <s>Quota exhaustion</s>: the reseller's upstream key burned its image quota for the day and now answers <c>429</c>. <s>Slug variants</s>: the same underlying model is exposed as <c>gpt-image-2</c>, <c>gpt-image-2-all</c>, <c>gpt-image-2-c</c>, and <c>gpt-image-2-vip</c> across different resellers, and only some of those slugs are actually wired to a working backend. <s>Endpoint mismatch</s>: a few resellers expose the slug but never plumbed <c>/v1/images/edits</c>, so the request 404s.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.GOTCHAS_P2: This is why we test continuously and route around failing channels at request time. A model that passes today can start 429-ing tomorrow if its reseller's upstream rotates. Static availability lists go stale fast in this corner of the market.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.H_METADATA: maxImageInputs is now in every model's metadata
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.METADATA_P1: Every image model in the catalog now carries a <c>maxImageInputs</c> field on its metadata block. Models that passed the 6-reference benchmark are tagged <c>maxImageInputs: 6</c>. The same shape is used by the catalog UI, the API, and the routing layer.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.METADATA_P2: If you only care about which models will accept your 6-image payload, filter on this field. New models added later get the same tag once they pass the same benchmark.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.TRY_P: Every model above is available through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Multi-reference image edit is exposed exactly as the upstream defines it, no extra wrapping. Bring six images and a prompt; the router picks a working provider.
SIX_INPUT_IMAGE_MODELS.CTA: <register>Grab an API key</register> or <models>browse the image catalog</models> to see the full verified list.

FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.TITLE: We aggregated 190+ free AI models into one endpoint
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.DESCRIPTION: We wired 18 free providers into {appName}: 190+ free model rows, one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, $0 per token. They carry upstream limits we cannot raise, plus a light 1-per-minute cap we add to keep the shared pools fair. Here is the honest version.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.AUTHOR: {appName} team
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.INTRO: The free-LLM landscape is real but scattered: Groq, Gemini, Cloudflare, NVIDIA, SiliconFlow and a dozen others each give away genuine capacity, behind a dozen signup pages, a dozen key formats, and a dozen incompatible APIs. We discovered, tested, and merged every legitimate permanent-free provider we could into {appName}. The result: 190+ free model rows from 18 providers behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint and one key.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.P_WHAT: Eighteen free providers, one at a time: Groq, Gemini, Cerebras, SambaNova, Mistral, Cloudflare Workers AI (two accounts), GitHub Models, Z.ai, OVHcloud, AI Horde, Pollinations, Cohere, Jina, NVIDIA NIM (full open catalog: Nemotron, Llama, Qwen, gpt-oss, DeepSeek and more), SiliconFlow (DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.1, Qwen3.5/3.6, Kimi-K2.6, MiniMax-M3), the HuggingFace router, and LLM7. That is 190+ free model rows: Llama, gpt-oss, Qwen, Mistral, GLM, Nemotron, DeepSeek and more, plus free embedding, image, and audio models. Every one is probed end to end for HTTP, streaming, and tool calls before it goes live, the same authenticity and harness checks we run on paid models.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.P_CAVEAT: These models are genuinely free, and that is exactly why they have limits. Each upstream enforces its own: requests per minute, daily token quotas, Cloudflare neuron budgets, volunteer-queue priority. Hit a cap and that provider returns <c>429</c> until it resets. A free key that worked this morning can be exhausted by this afternoon. Free tier is best-effort throughput, not a guarantee. If your workload needs predictable latency and no surprise <c>429</c>s, use a paid model.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.P_AGGREGATE: Because the alternative is eighteen accounts. Each provider has its own signup, its own key format, its own base URL, and its own quirks: Z.ai speaks the Zhipu V4 path, Cloudflare carries the account id in the URL, AI Horde wants an anonymous key, GitHub gates models behind a token scope, the HuggingFace router fans out across a dozen upstreams. We absorbed all of that so you call them the way you call everything else: one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, one key, a model name. The honest rule we hold ourselves to: one real account per provider, caps accepted, nothing farmed, nothing pooled. We expose the free tier as a gift, not as a resale of someone else's quota.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.P_FAILOVER: Many of these models are served by more than one free provider. Llama 3.3 70B alone runs on seven of them. When several providers offer the same model, we collapse them into one published name and fail over automatically: if one upstream returns a <c>429</c> or goes quiet, the next healthy provider serving that model takes the request. That is the one lever we do control. If every provider for a model is momentarily rate-limited, the request returns an HTTP <c>503</c> with an explicit "all providers busy" message (not a 404, and not "model not found"), and the channel is re-tested and re-enabled within minutes by our health cron. So a multi-source free model keeps answering long after any one of its providers is exhausted. Single-source free models have no fallback, so they stall when their one upstream is spent.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.P_HONEST: We did not add reverse proxies that re-serve OpenAI or Claude flagships without permission. We did not pull in personal-key aggregators whose tokens are non-transferable, or pool-of-pools services that farm and rotate other people's keys. Those exist and they are tempting and they are exactly the gray-market mess this gateway is meant to replace. Every provider on the list gives its free tier away on purpose, under its own terms. If a source could not pass that bar, it is not here.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.CTA: All 190+ free models are live behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. <register>Grab an API key</register> or <models>browse the model catalog</models> and filter for free. Just remember which tier you are on when a <c>429</c> or <c>503</c> shows up.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.H_LIMIT: Our own rate limit, and why it is there
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.P_LIMIT: On top of the upstream caps we add a small limit of our own: <s>one request per minute per free model, per user</s>. It is deliberate. A single free model is often one shared upstream pool of maybe a million tokens a day for everyone combined, so without a cap a handful of heavy users would drain it in minutes and everyone else would see nothing. One per minute per model keeps the pool alive and spread across the whole community, and you can spread traffic across the many free models rather than hammering one. When you hit our cap you get an HTTP <c>429</c> with a <c>Retry-After</c> header telling you exactly how long to wait. This is separate from the upstream <c>429</c> and from the <c>503</c> below. If you want higher throughput on a specific model, use its paid tier where the limit does not apply.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.TLDR: {appName} aggregates free lanes from many upstream providers into more than 190 models with a genuine free tier behind one key. Each free model allows about 1 request per minute per user; hitting the cap returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header, and drained pools return an explicit all providers busy error and recover automatically. Paid models bill pay as you go from $1.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.FAQ_1_Q: How many free models does {appName} have?
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.FAQ_1_A: More than 190 at any moment, out of a catalog of 200+ models. The exact set shifts as upstream free pools drain and recover, and the live list is at unorouter.com/models.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.FAQ_2_Q: What are the free tier rate limits?
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.FAQ_2_A: About 1 request per minute per model per user. The cap returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header. With 190+ free models the practical answer is to rotate models instead of waiting.
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.FAQ_3_Q: Do I need a credit card for the free models?
FREE_MODELS_AGGREGATED.FAQ_3_A: No. Sign up with Discord or GitHub, create a key, and use any model with the :free suffix. A one time $1 Discord verify bonus can be spent on the paid models.

UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.TITLE: {appName} vs OpenRouter: an honest comparison
UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.DESCRIPTION: {appName} and OpenRouter both put many models behind one OpenAI-compatible key. The difference is what sits on top: a headless API, or an API plus a built-in chat and character client. Here is the honest version.
UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.AUTHOR: {appName} team
UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.INTRO: OpenRouter gives you one key for every model. So does {appName}. The difference fits in one line: OpenRouter is just the API, {appName} is the API plus a built-in chat and character client on the same key. That is the whole comparison.
UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.H_LANES: API, or API plus a client
UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.P_LANES: OpenRouter, LiteLLM, and Portkey hand you an endpoint and stop. You build the interface yourself. {appName} ships both: a clean API for coding agents, and a chat and character client that share one key, one catalog, one balance.
UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.P_MODELS: Both put 200+ models behind one key with no markup on tokens. OpenRouter charges a 5.5% fee when you buy credits (with an $0.80 minimum), and its free models are capped at 50 requests a day until you have bought $10 of credits. {appName} is pay-as-you-go, no purchase fee, credits never expire, and the free tier is open from the start. The catalogs are close, so the catalog is not what decides it.
UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.P_RP: Point Claude Code, Cline, or Codex at {appName} and it just works like any OpenAI endpoint. The same key also runs a full character client (personas, lorebooks, presets, SillyTavern card import) and drops into SillyTavern, Janitor.AI, or Chub. OpenRouter is API-only, so every interface is on you.
UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.P_MIGRATE: Point your client at <c>https://api.unorouter.com/v1</c> and keep your code. The same key works in a chat app's custom-endpoint field, so there is no second account to manage.
UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.P_VERDICT: Only shipping code and want the widest catalog? OpenRouter is fine. Want zero-markup self-hosted routing? Use LiteLLM. Want one key that runs your coding agent and a real chat client? That is {appName}.
UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.CTA: Ready to try it? <register>Create a free account</register> or <models>browse the models</models>.
UNOROUTER_VS_OPENROUTER.TLDR: {appName} and OpenRouter both put 200+ models behind one OpenAI compatible key. OpenRouter is API only and closed source. {appName} adds a built in chat and character client on the same key, publishes its full stack under OSI licenses, and serves most models on a genuine free tier of about 1 request per minute per model. Paid use is pay as you go and credits never expire.

WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.TITLE: What is an LLM gateway?
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.DESCRIPTION: An LLM gateway is one endpoint and key that routes requests to many model providers. Here is what it does, why it helps, and who actually needs one.
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.AUTHOR: {appName} team
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.INTRO: An LLM gateway is a single API endpoint that sits in front of many model providers and routes your request to whichever model you ask for. Instead of holding a separate key, base URL, and SDK quirk for each lab, you hold one key and one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and the gateway handles the rest. It is the same idea as an API gateway in classic backend work, applied to language models. Here is what that buys you.
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.P_DEFINITION: A gateway exposes one OpenAI-compatible interface, usually <c>/v1/chat/completions</c>, and maps the <c>model</c> field in your request to a real provider behind the scenes. You send the same request shape every time; the gateway picks the upstream, attaches the right provider credentials, translates any quirks, and streams the response back. Your code does not change when you switch models, because the contract you code against stays constant.
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.P_WHY_IT_HELPS: Three wins. One integration: write against one endpoint and you can use every model the gateway carries, with no per-provider client. One bill: usage across all providers lands on a single balance instead of a dozen separate invoices. And easy switching: changing a model is a one-line edit, so you can chase the best price or quality per task without re-plumbing your app. For most builders the time saved on integration alone is the whole reason.
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.H_HOW_IT_WORKS: How it works under the hood
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.P_HOW_IT_WORKS: When a request arrives, the gateway reads the <c>model</c> name, looks up the matching upstream provider, swaps in that provider's credentials, rewrites any provider-specific body fields, and forwards the call. The streamed tokens come back through the same connection, so from your side it looks like one normal OpenAI call. Good gateways add retries on transient errors, usage and cost accounting, and a current model catalog so new releases appear without you touching anything.
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.P_WHO_NEEDS_ONE: You want a gateway if you use more than one model, plan to switch models as prices and quality move, or build anything that should not be hard-wired to a single lab. Coding agents, chat apps, character chat front ends, and internal tools all benefit. If you genuinely only ever call one model from one provider and never expect to change, a direct provider key is simpler. Everyone else saves real effort with a gateway.
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.P_VERDICT: An LLM gateway turns many providers into one endpoint, one key, and one bill, so you integrate once and switch models freely. {appName} is an OpenAI-compatible gateway in exactly this mold: one key reaches 200+ models for code and chat alike, with pay-as-you-go credits that do not expire. If you touch more than one model, a gateway is the cleaner foundation.
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.CTA: Try a gateway yourself: <register>create a free account</register> or <models>browse the models</models>.
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.TLDR: An LLM gateway is one API in front of many model providers: one key, one bill, one endpoint, with routing and failover handled for you. {appName} is an open source gateway serving 200+ models through an OpenAI compatible API, plus Anthropic and Gemini native endpoints, with a free tier on most models and pay as you go pricing on the rest.
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.FAQ_1_Q: When do I need an LLM gateway instead of a direct provider key?
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.FAQ_1_A: When you use more than one model family, want failover when a provider is down, or want one bill. A gateway removes per vendor accounts and lets you switch models by changing one string.
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.FAQ_2_Q: Does an LLM gateway add latency?
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.FAQ_2_A: One extra hop, typically tens of milliseconds, which streaming hides in practice. Slow responses come from the model itself far more often than from the gateway.
WHAT_IS_AN_LLM_GATEWAY.FAQ_3_A: OpenAI compatible /v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses and /v1/embeddings, Anthropic native /v1/messages, and Gemini native /v1beta, all behind one key.

JANITOR_AI.TITLE: Janitor.AI Integration Guide
JANITOR_AI.SUBTITLE: Connect {appName} to Janitor.AI as a custom proxy with the exact URL format Janitor''s API Settings panel expects.
JANITOR_AI.INTRO_DESC: Janitor.AI is a browser-based character chat platform. It ships a built-in free model and lets you add any OpenAI-compatible proxy for unlimited access. {appName} plugs in at the API Settings panel.
JANITOR_AI.OVERVIEW_DESC: Janitor.AI calls your proxy at the FULL `/v1/chat/completions` URL. You paste that URL, your API key, and the model name into a configuration, hit Save, then hard-refresh the browser for the configuration to activate.
JANITOR_AI.QUICK_CONFIG_DESC: Copy these three values into the Add Configuration panel in Janitor.AI.
JANITOR_AI.QUICK_CONFIG_NOTE: Paste the full URL ending in `/v1/chat/completions`, not just the base URL. If Janitor shows an 'Add /chat/completions to URL' checkbox, leave it OFF.
JANITOR_AI.WARN_REFRESH_DESC: After you click Save Settings, Janitor.AI will not activate the new proxy until the browser reloads. Press Ctrl+Shift+R (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Shift+R (macOS) before sending a test message. This is the single most common reason a freshly saved proxy appears broken.
JANITOR_AI.STEP_1_DESC: Start any chat and click the gear icon at the top-right of the chat view.
JANITOR_AI.STEP_2_DESC: Select API Settings, then click Add Configuration.
JANITOR_AI.STEP_3_DESC: Config Name (anything), Model Name (from {appName}''s models page), Proxy URL (the full `/v1/chat/completions` URL), API Key.
JANITOR_AI.STEP_4_DESC: Save the configuration into the list of available proxies.
JANITOR_AI.STEP_6_DESC: Press Ctrl+Shift+R or Cmd+Shift+R. The proxy only activates after a full page reload.
JANITOR_AI.REFRESH_SAVE_DESC: Janitor.AI caches the proxy map at page load. Saving rewrites local storage but the already-loaded app still holds the old map. The hard-refresh forces Janitor to re-read the fresh configuration.
JANITOR_AI.KEY_INVISIBILITY_DESC: Janitor.AI masks the API key field after save; you cannot copy it back out. Store the key in a password manager before you paste it, so rotation or a second browser profile does not require a new key generation.
JANITOR_AI.TS_1_TITLE: A 'Free tier limit reached' banner appears.
JANITOR_AI.TS_1_DESC: That banner is Janitor''s built-in tier, not {appName}. Switch the chat to your saved proxy configuration in the model dropdown at the top of the chat.
JANITOR_AI.TS_2_TITLE: Proxy does not respond after save.
JANITOR_AI.TS_2_DESC: You did not hard-refresh. Press Ctrl+Shift+R or Cmd+Shift+R and retry.
JANITOR_AI.TS_3_DESC: The Proxy URL is missing the `/v1/chat/completions` suffix. Re-open the configuration and paste the full URL.
JANITOR_AI.TS_4_DESC: Wrong API key. Janitor hid the old key, so delete the configuration and recreate it with a fresh key from your password manager or the {appName} dashboard.
JANITOR_AI.TS_5_DESC: Increase Max Tokens in Janitor's Generation Settings. This is not a proxy issue; it is a Janitor-side output limit.
JANITOR_AI.TS_6_TITLE: Wrong model replies, or a 'model not found' error.
JANITOR_AI.TS_6_DESC: The Model Name field must match a model ID exactly. Copy-paste from {appName}''s models page rather than retyping.
JANITOR_AI.CTA_DESC: Get your {appName} API key and run Janitor.AI against every model we support.

RISUAI.TITLE: RisuAI Integration Guide
RISUAI.SUBTITLE: Connect {appName} to RisuAI through the Custom Models option in Advanced Settings.
RISUAI.INTRO_DESC: RisuAI is a local-first character chat frontend that runs in the browser or as a desktop app. It supports any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with configuration stored in browser local storage.
RISUAI.INTRO_WIKI_NOTE: The official RisuAI wiki is behind the current UI. Steps below reflect RisuAI as of 2026-04.
RISUAI.OVERVIEW_DESC: RisuAI's Custom Models slot lets you paste a Request URL, API key, and model ID. The gotcha is a toggle called Autofill Request URL: when it is on, RisuAI rewrites the URL you paste, which silently breaks the connection.
RISUAI.WARN_AUTOFILL_TITLE: Uncheck Autofill Request URL before pasting
RISUAI.WARN_AUTOFILL_DESC: If Autofill Request URL is on, RisuAI rewrites whatever URL you paste into its own default format, which breaks the connection with no error. Uncheck this toggle BEFORE you paste the Request URL. This is the single most common reason a RisuAI + custom proxy setup fails.
RISUAI.QUICK_CONFIG_DESC: Copy these three values into the Custom Models fields in RisuAI's Advanced Settings.
RISUAI.QUICK_CONFIG_NOTE: Paste the full URL ending in `/v1/chat/completions`. RisuAI has no model dropdown in Custom Models mode; the Model ID is a manual text field.
RISUAI.STEP_1_DESC: In RisuAI, open Settings, then Advanced Settings.
RISUAI.STEP_2_DESC: Click the Chat Bot model selector, scroll to the bottom of the model list, and choose Custom Models.
RISUAI.STEP_3_DESC: This toggle must be OFF before you paste anything. See the critical warning above.
RISUAI.STEP_4_DESC: Paste the full URL ending in `/v1/chat/completions`.
RISUAI.STEP_5_DESC: Paste your {appName} API key into the API Key field. Some RisuAI builds label this field Authorization; use that field if the API Key field does not appear.
RISUAI.STEP_6_DESC: Type or paste the exact model name from {appName}''s models page.
RISUAI.STEP_7_DESC: Close the settings panel; RisuAI writes configuration to local storage.
RISUAI.STEP_8_DESC: Open any chat and send a test message to verify the response.
RISUAI.AUTOFILL_WARNING_DETAIL_DESC: Autofill Request URL was added to prevent typos against named preset providers. For Custom Models, it becomes a foot-gun: RisuAI rewrites your custom URL to a default that does not point at us. If a RisuAI update flips this toggle back on, redo step 3 before debugging anything else.
RISUAI.AUX_MODEL_DESC: RisuAI uses a second model slot for translation, summary, and name-guessing tasks. Repeat steps 2 through 7 for the Auxiliary Model selector, using the same {appName} URL and key.
RISUAI.TS_1_DESC: Autofill Request URL was on when you pasted; RisuAI rewrote the URL. Uncheck the toggle and re-paste the Request URL.
RISUAI.TS_2_DESC: A RisuAI update can re-enable Autofill Request URL silently. Open Custom Models and confirm it is still off.
RISUAI.TS_3_DESC: RisuAI builds sometimes expose both API Key and Authorization fields; only one is read depending on version. Move your key to the other field and retry.
RISUAI.TS_4_DESC: The Model ID must match a model name exactly. Copy-paste from {appName}''s models page; do not retype.
RISUAI.TS_5_TITLE: Translation or summary feature is broken.
RISUAI.TS_5_DESC: The Auxiliary Model is unconfigured. Repeat setup for the Auxiliary Model slot.
RISUAI.TS_6_TITLE: Streaming output is chunked or missing pieces.
RISUAI.TS_6_DESC: RisuAI's SSE parser expects plain `data:` events. A corporate proxy stripping the prefix will produce garbled streaming. Test on a non-corporate network if available.
RISUAI.TS_7_DESC: RisuAI stores configuration in browser local storage, which some privacy modes clear. Export your config to a file from Settings for backup.
RISUAI.CTA_DESC: Get your {appName} API key and run RisuAI against every model we support.
RISUAI.GOTCHA_1: Uncheck Autofill Request URL before you paste anything. While it is on, RisuAI rewrites your URL to its own default and silently breaks the connection.
RISUAI.GOTCHA_2: A RisuAI update can re-enable Autofill Request URL on its own. If a working setup suddenly stops responding, re-open Custom Models and confirm the toggle is still off.
RISUAI.GOTCHA_3: Some RisuAI builds expose both an API Key field and an Authorization field, and only one is read per version. If you get a 401, move your key to the other field.
RISUAI.GOTCHA_4: The Model ID is a manual text field with no dropdown in Custom Models mode. Copy-paste the exact model name from {appName}''s models page; do not retype it.

CHUB.STEP_7_DESC: Set the API dropdown to OpenAI, then select your target model from the model dropdown.

CHUB.TS_4_DESC: Your API key was rotated or typo''d. Generate a new key at your {appName} dashboard, then re-paste into Reverse proxy.
CHUB.TS_5_DESC: Lower the max context in Prompt Structure, or pick a model with a larger context on {appName}''s models page.
CHUB.TS_6_TITLE: After reload the proxy check says pass but messages fail.
CHUB.TS_6_DESC: Chub caches the proxy-check state across sessions. Press Check your proxy once on a new session to force a fresh check.
CHUB.CTA_DESC: Get your {appName} API key and run Chub / Venus against every model we support.
CHUB.STEP_CONFIG_DESC: Return to the hamburger menu, open Configuration, then Prompt Structure. Set the API dropdown to OpenAI and select your target model from the model dropdown.

CHUB.GOTCHA_2: The model dropdown in Prompt Structure stays empty until the proxy check passes. Run Check your proxy in Secrets first, then return to pick a model.

RULES.NOT_FRAUD_TITLE: What is NOT counted as fake
RULES.PROOF: This whole tester is open source. Read exactly which probes run and why:

CODING-TOOL.TITLE: Coding-tool wrapper
CODING-TOOL.MEANS: The reply uses canned phrases from a coding assistant (Kiro, Cascade, Codeium and similar), refusing an ordinary creative or emotional prompt.
CODING-TOOL.WHY: A real Claude/GPT/Gemini answers a kitten story or a haiku. A coding-tool distill refuses it, which exposes a substituted model behind the endpoint.
CODING-TOOL.EXCEPTION: the model simply declines for a safety reason without the coding-assistant boilerplate.

SCAM.TITLE: Scam / token-theft page
SCAM.MEANS: The response contains known token-theft or phishing text instead of a model answer.
SCAM.WHY: An endpoint returning a scam landing page is not serving a model at all.
SCAM.EXCEPTION: the model legitimately discusses the word "token" in a normal answer.

CJK-LEAK.TITLE: Unexpected language leak
CJK-LEAK.MEANS: An English-only prompt comes back with four or more CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) characters.
CJK-LEAK.WHY: A leak of CJK into an English answer is a strong tell of a substituted Chinese model or a corrupting proxy, even when the identity question is answered correctly.
CJK-LEAK.EXCEPTION: you asked in or about a CJK language, so CJK in the reply is expected.

MUX.TITLE: Response mixing (unsafe proxy)
MUX.MEANS: Each probe carries a unique nonce. Two or more replies come back without the nonce we sent, after retries.
MUX.WHY: A proxy that multiplexes one request across several upstreams returns answers that do not match the request we made, which an honest single-model endpoint never does.
MUX.EXCEPTION: a single nonce miss happens once (we retry first), so only repeated mismatches count.

FOREIGN.TITLE: Foreign vendor identity
FOREIGN.MEANS: On the identity or model-name probe the reply names a different vendor than requested (for example OpenAI or Gemini when Claude was asked for).
FOREIGN.WHY: A model naming a rival lab as its maker is being served by that rival, not the one you paid for.
FOREIGN.EXCEPTION: the model is vague about its version or declines to name itself, which real models often do.

TIER-MISMATCH.TITLE: Tier downgrade (Claude)
TIER-MISMATCH.MEANS: You requested one Claude tier (Opus) but the model names a cheaper tier (Sonnet or Haiku).
TIER-MISMATCH.WHY: Claude may be vague about its exact version but never confuses its tier, so a named lower tier is a deliberate downgrade.
TIER-MISMATCH.EXCEPTION: the model is unsure of its version number. Only a clearly named different tier counts.

VERSION.TITLE: Version vagueness
VERSION.BODY: a genuine model confirms the vendor and tier but is often unsure of its exact version. That alone is never a fail, only marked as advisory.

TRANSIENT.TITLE: Temporary errors
TRANSIENT.BODY: rate limits (429), 5xx and timeouts mark a run as unverified, never suspicious. A real endpoint having a bad moment is not penalised.

CLOUD-HOST.TITLE: Cloud host names
CLOUD-HOST.BODY: naming AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex or Azure as the host is accepted, since those are legitimate ways to resell the real model.

RESHAPING.TITLE: Protocol reshaping
RESHAPING.BODY: translating between chat-completions and the native messages format is normal gateway behaviour and is not a fraud signal when the model itself is genuine.

THRESHOLD.TITLE: One flaky probe
THRESHOLD.BODY: three of four probes passing is enough to be genuine, so a single off answer does not condemn an honest endpoint.

RULES.COMMUNITY: Have an idea for a better probe? Suggest one here:

KEY_SAFE.A: For a local test the key never leaves your browser, it is sent straight to the endpoint you entered. Only when you choose to publish does the key go to our server, which runs the test in memory and never stores it. Use a throwaway key if in doubt.

SERVER_PROXY.Q: Why does it sometimes need a server proxy?
SERVER_PROXY.A: Some endpoints block direct browser requests (<cors>CORS</cors>). When that happens we offer an optional backend test that relays the probes for you. Publishing always runs server-side so the public result cannot be forged.

RELIABILITY.A: Detection is deterministic, not a machine-learning guess. Each probe either matches a concrete signal or it does not, and the result shows you the exact evidence. We require three of four probes to pass and treat temporary errors as unverified, not as failures.

FALSE_POSITIVE.Q: How do I report a false positive?
FALSE_POSITIVE.A: Every published result is disputable. If you publish it yourself while logged in you can delete it directly. Otherwise open a <ghIssue>GitHub issue</ghIssue> or message us on <discord>Discord</discord> and we will re-check and remove wrong entries.

PROTOCOLS.A: Anthropic (/v1/messages), OpenAI (/v1/chat/completions) and Google Gemini (generateContent). We try the provider's native format first and fall back to the OpenAI-compatible format if needed.

OPEN_SOURCE.A: Yes. This tester runs entirely in your browser and its detection library is public on <gh>GitHub</gh>, so you can read exactly which probes run and why, suggest new ones, or discuss them on <discord>Discord</discord>.

GAUGE.RUNNING_HINT: Running the probes against your endpoint.
GAUGE.DONE_HINT: Each arc is one probe. Expand a probe below to see the prompt, the reply, and the evidence.

WHY.TITLE: Why this tester is different
WHY.DETERMINISTIC_BODY: Each check matches a concrete signal in the reply, so we don't flag real models as fake the way statistical fingerprinting does. Read the exact code.
WHY.VERIFIED_BODY: A result only reaches the public board after our server re-runs the whole test itself, so the rankings cannot be forged.
WHY.EVIDENCE_BODY: Every verdict shows the prompt sent, the raw reply, and the matched text that triggered it. Nothing is hidden.

EMOTIONAL.CHECKS: Asks for a short, emotionally grounded story.
EMOTIONAL.WHY: A genuine frontier model writes real empathetic prose. A coding-tool distill or cheap substitute refuses it or returns flat, canned text.

CREATIVE.CHECKS: Asks for a haiku or short poem in a fixed form.
CREATIVE.WHY: Real Claude, GPT and Gemini hold poetic form. A substituted model breaks the form, ignores the constraint, or declines.

IDENTITY.CHECKS: Asks which AI lab trained the model, in one word.
IDENTITY.WHY: The answer should name the expected lab. A different lab, or a coding-assistant identity, exposes a swapped backend behind the endpoint.

MODEL-NAME.CHECKS: Asks the model to state its own model name.
MODEL-NAME.WHY: A wrong, vague or refused name signals the endpoint is not serving the model it advertises.

GETTING_STARTED.P_OVERVIEW_1: The chat is a full roleplay engine in your browser. Characters, personas, lorebooks, presets, and every conversation live in a local database on your device; the server only relays model requests. You can use any catalog model or bring your own provider.
GETTING_STARTED.P_OVERVIEW_2: Open the chat from the top navigation. A new conversation starts on the chat home screen; everything you equip there can be changed later per conversation.
GETTING_STARTED.P_LOADOUT_1: The loadout is the sticky set of preset, persona, characters, and lorebooks that auto-equips on every new chat. Set it once on the chat home screen and each new conversation starts ready to go.
GETTING_STARTED.P_LOADOUT_2: Per-conversation overrides live in the settings drawer inside the chat: swap the persona, add lorebooks, change sampling, or toggle features without touching your loadout.
GETTING_STARTED.P_GREETINGS_1: A character's first message opens the chat. If the card ships alternate greetings, a preview picker appears before your first send so you can choose the opening you like.
GETTING_STARTED.P_GREETINGS_2: Greetings are macro-expanded once, so {appName} fills in names and random values at insertion time. Each greeting is a root branch: swiping on the first message switches between them.
GETTING_STARTED.P_MESSAGES_1: Every reply can be regenerated. Regenerations become siblings of the original message, and you swipe between them; nothing is overwritten.
GETTING_STARTED.P_MESSAGES_2: Conversations are trees, not lists. Editing or regenerating in the middle creates a new branch, and the previous line of the story stays intact and reachable.
GETTING_STARTED.P_MESSAGES_3: A failed send stays in the timeline so you can retry manually; nothing is silently resent. Offline sends are marked as queued.
GETTING_STARTED.P_AUTOCONTINUE_1: With auto-continue enabled, a reply that stops mid-sentence automatically requests a continuation, up to three times. Toggle it per conversation in the settings drawer.
GETTING_STARTED.P_NEXT_1: Import a character card, create a persona, and skim the Presets page to understand how the prompt is assembled. The Lorebooks and Macros pages unlock the deeper systems.
GETTING_STARTED.P_NEXT_2: opens search across all docs pages.

META.TITLE: Character Cards in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: Create, import, and export character cards: fields, avatars, prompt overrides, PNG and CHARX import, and four export formats.
META.KEYWORDS: character card, import png card, charx, character editor, sillytavern card, export character

CHARACTERS.TITLE: Characters
CHARACTERS.SUBTITLE: Create, import, and export character cards.
CHARACTERS.P_FIELDS_1: A character card is a set of text fields that become part of the prompt. All fields support macros.
CHARACTERS.F_NAME_DESC: The character's display name; also what the char macro resolves to.
CHARACTERS.F_DESCRIPTION_DESC: The main body of who the character is. The largest single block sent to the model.
CHARACTERS.F_PERSONALITY_DESC: Short trait summary appended to the character block.
CHARACTERS.F_SCENARIO_DESC: The setting or situation the chat starts in.
CHARACTERS.F_FIRST_MESSAGE_DESC: The opening message. Alternate greetings add swipeable variants.
CHARACTERS.F_EXAMPLES_DESC: Sample dialogue parsed into few-shot turns that teach the model the character's voice.
CHARACTERS.F_AVATAR_DESC: Images for the chat UI. The avatar can also feed image generation as a reference.
CHARACTERS.P_PROMPT_FIELDS_1: Two advanced fields override preset prompts for this character only: a system prompt that replaces the preset's system slot, and post-history instructions injected after the chat history, where they have the strongest effect on the next reply.
CHARACTERS.P_PROMPT_FIELDS_2: Leave both empty unless the card needs special steering; preset-level prompts cover the normal case.
CHARACTERS.P_BEHAVIOR_1: Each character carries its own trigger scripts, turn triggers, and regex scripts, so a card can ship its own automation. See the Scripting section for how these run.
CHARACTERS.P_BEHAVIOR_2: In group chats, always active controls whether the character's block is always in the prompt or only when the character is talking or mentioned; match whole words tightens name-mention detection. A per-character reasoning effort default applies when the model supports it.
CHARACTERS.P_IMPORT_1: Import PNG cards (spec v2 and v3), CHARX archives, and plain JSON. Drop the file on the characters page or use the import button; embedded avatars and greetings come along.
CHARACTERS.P_IMPORT_2: Cards from SillyTavern, RisuAI, and hub sites work as-is. Unknown extra fields are preserved where the spec allows so a later export does not lose them.
CHARACTERS.P_EXPORT_1: Export any character in four formats:
CHARACTERS.X_PNG: The universal card format; works in SillyTavern, RisuAI, and most frontends.
CHARACTERS.X_CHARX: The v3 archive format; keeps multiple assets alongside the card data.
CHARACTERS.X_VOXTA: For the Voxta voice roleplay app.
CHARACTERS.X_JSON: Raw card data for editing or tooling.

PERSONAS.TITLE: Personas
PERSONAS.SUBTITLE: The identity you play as in every chat.
PERSONAS.P_FIELDS_1: A persona is who you are in the story: a name, an optional display-only title shown in lists, a description the model sees, and an avatar for the UI. The user macro resolves to the persona name, and the persona description is injected into its own prompt slot.
PERSONAS.P_FIELDS_2: Keep the description in third person and reasonably short; it is sent with every message.
PERSONAS.P_DEFAULT_1: Mark one persona as default and every new chat starts with it. You can still swap personas per conversation in the settings drawer, and the loadout can pin a different one.
PERSONAS.P_IMPORT_1: Personas import from persona files exported by other frontends. Duplicating an existing persona is often the fastest way to create a variant.

META.TITLE: Lorebooks in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: World info that activates on keywords: entries, activation logic, priority and order, injection roles, decorators, and token budgets.
META.KEYWORDS: lorebook, world info, keyword activation, decorators, token budget, recursive scanning

LOREBOOKS.TITLE: Lorebooks
LOREBOOKS.SUBTITLE: World knowledge that appears in the prompt exactly when it is relevant.
LOREBOOKS.P_BOOKS_1: A lorebook is a collection of entries plus scan settings. Attach any number of books to a conversation; all attached books scan together as one pool.
LOREBOOKS.S_SCAN_DEPTH: How many recent messages are scanned for keywords. Both your messages and the character's count.
LOREBOOKS.S_TOKEN_BUDGET: Cap on the total tokens of activated entries. When books disagree, the highest budget wins.
LOREBOOKS.S_RECURSIVE: Activated entry content is scanned again, letting lore activate more lore (up to 3 passes).
LOREBOOKS.P_ENTRIES_1: An entry has keys (comma-separated trigger words), optional secondary keys, and content. When any key appears in the scanned history, the entry activates and its content is injected.
LOREBOOKS.P_ENTRIES_2: Selective mode requires a primary AND a secondary key to match. Constant entries skip matching and are always injected. Disabled entries stay in the book but never fire. Match whole words prevents fire from matching campfire.
LOREBOOKS.P_ENTRIES_3: Each entry has a display name (comment) used only for organizing the editor list; it is never sent to the model and survives import/export round-trips.
LOREBOOKS.P_ORDERING_1: Two numbers control an entry's fate. Priority decides who survives the token budget: higher priority entries are kept first when space runs out.
LOREBOOKS.P_ORDERING_2: Order (insertion order) decides placement among the survivors: higher order appears earlier in the prompt. Same order falls back to priority, then entry id.
LOREBOOKS.P_INJECTION_1: All activated entries render into a single lorebook slot in the prompt template, each as its own message with its chosen role: system, user, or assistant.
LOREBOOKS.P_INJECTION_2: There is no per-entry position concept; move the lorebook slot in the prompt template editor to control where lore lands relative to everything else.
LOREBOOKS.P_DECORATORS_1: Lines starting with @@ at the top of entry content tweak that entry's behavior:
LOREBOOKS.D_PROBABILITY: Percent chance to inject when activated; the roll is stable within a turn.
LOREBOOKS.D_SCAN_DEPTH: Override the book's scan depth for this entry.
LOREBOOKS.D_ORDER: Override placement order or budget priority for this entry.
LOREBOOKS.D_ROLE: Override the injection role for this entry.
LOREBOOKS.D_ACTIVATE: Fire only after N messages, or only every N messages.
LOREBOOKS.D_STICKY: Keep an entry active after its first match, or never activate again after a match.
LOREBOOKS.D_GREETING: Only active while the chat is still on the greeting message.
LOREBOOKS.P_BUDGET_1: Token counting uses the active model's tokenizer, so the budget reflects what the model actually sees. When entries exceed the budget, the lowest-priority entries are dropped first.
LOREBOOKS.P_BUDGET_2: If lore keeps getting cut, raise the budget, lower entry priority spread, or shorten entries. The request log shows exactly which entries made it into a given request.

CARDS.TITLE: Cards
CARDS.SUBTITLE: Bundle persona, characters, and lorebooks into one loadout.
CARDS.P_CONCEPT_1: A card bundles a persona, a set of characters, and a set of lorebooks under one name. Think of it as a saved scenario setup: one click restores the whole table.
CARDS.P_CONCEPT_2: Cards reference entities, they do not copy them: editing a character later is reflected in every card that includes it.
CARDS.P_APPLY_1: Apply a card in replace mode to make the chat's equipment exactly match the card, or merge mode to add the card's entities on top of what is already equipped.
CARDS.P_APPLY_2: Applying only changes the current conversation's equipment; your sticky loadout on the chat home stays as it was.
CARDS.P_EXPORT_1: Cards export as JSON bundles for backup or sharing; import restores the card with new local ids.

META.TITLE: Presets in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: Sampling parameters, request behavior toggles, and the main, post-history, and prefill prompts that shape every request.
META.KEYWORDS: preset, temperature, sampler settings, main prompt, prefill, post history

PRESETS.TITLE: Presets
PRESETS.SUBTITLE: The request recipe: sampling, behavior toggles, and core prompts.
PRESETS.P_SAMPLING_1: Presets carry the full sampler set: temperature, top-p, frequency and presence penalties, max output tokens, and reasoning effort where supported. Conversation-level sliders override the preset for that chat only.
PRESETS.P_SAMPLING_2: Extra body lets you pass provider-specific JSON fields verbatim; on key clash it beats the preset, and sliders beat both.
PRESETS.P_BEHAVIOR_1: Toggles adapt the request to strict providers and special workflows:
PRESETS.B_NO_SYSTEM_ROLE: Rewrites system messages as user messages for endpoints that reject the system role.
PRESETS.B_FORCE_ALTERNATE: Merges consecutive same-role messages so roles strictly alternate.
PRESETS.B_USER_FIRST: Prepends a stub user turn when the history would otherwise start with the assistant.
PRESETS.B_GEMINI_BLOCK_OFF: Sets all Gemini safety categories to OFF.
PRESETS.B_STREAMING: Streams tokens as they generate instead of waiting for the full reply.
PRESETS.B_SHOW_REASONING: Shows model reasoning blocks in the UI when the model emits them.
PRESETS.P_PROMPTS_1: The main prompt opens the request and carries your global instructions. It supports macros, so one preset adapts to any character.
PRESETS.P_PROMPTS_2: Post-history instructions are injected after the chat history with a configurable role; being last gives them the strongest pull on the next reply.
PRESETS.P_PROMPTS_3: Prefill seeds the start of the assistant's answer, useful for steering models that support assistant-side continuation.
PRESETS.P_DEFAULT_1: Mark a preset as default for new chats, and pin a different one in the loadout when a scenario needs its own recipe. Duplicate a preset before experimenting; switching back is one click.

META.TITLE: Prompt Template Editor in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: Drag-reorder the blocks of the assembled prompt: slots, plain blocks, and the chat history marker.
META.KEYWORDS: prompt template, prompt order, prompt blocks, custom prompt structure

PROMPT_TEMPLATE.TITLE: Prompt Template
PROMPT_TEMPLATE.SUBTITLE: Reorder what the model sees, block by block.
PROMPT_TEMPLATE.P_CONCEPT_1: Every request is assembled from blocks: prompts, character data, lore, persona, and the chat history. The prompt template editor in the preset lets you reorder those blocks by dragging.
PROMPT_TEMPLATE.P_CONCEPT_2: No template means the default order; the template only exists when you customize it, and removing it restores the default exactly.
PROMPT_TEMPLATE.P_BLOCKS_1: Slot blocks stand for engine-provided content: main prompt, persona, lorebook, system prompt, and prefill. They render whatever those systems produce at request time.
PROMPT_TEMPLATE.P_BLOCKS_2: Plain blocks are your own fixed text with a role of your choice, macro-expanded like everything else.
PROMPT_TEMPLATE.P_BLOCKS_3: The chat history marker places the conversation itself. Everything above it is pre-history; everything below lands after the history, post-history territory.
PROMPT_TEMPLATE.P_ORDER_2: Leading system messages are hoisted into the request's system parameter unless the preset disables the system role.
PROMPT_TEMPLATE.P_TIPS_1: Move the lorebook slot below character blocks when lore should override character facts; the later a block, the more the model weighs it.
PROMPT_TEMPLATE.P_TIPS_2: Use the dry-run inspector in the chat actions menu to preview the exact assembled prompt without spending tokens.

META.TITLE: Group Chats in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: Multiple characters in one conversation: speaker rotation, name-mention priority, and per-character prompt gating.
META.KEYWORDS: group chat, multiple characters, speaker rotation, turn order

GROUP_CHATS.TITLE: Group Chats
GROUP_CHATS.SUBTITLE: Several characters, one scene.
GROUP_CHATS.P_SETUP_1: Equip more than one character in the conversation settings drawer and the chat becomes a group scene. Each reply is generated as one specific character, tagged with the speaker.
GROUP_CHATS.P_ROTATION_1: After your message, the engine picks who answers: characters you mentioned by name get priority, then a weighted random pick based on each character's talkativeness, and nobody speaks twice back to back.
GROUP_CHATS.P_ROTATION_2: The roll is seeded per turn, so regenerating a reply keeps the same speaker instead of reshuffling the scene.
GROUP_CHATS.P_GATING_1: By default every equipped character's card data is in the prompt. Characters with always active off are gated: their block only appears when they speak or are mentioned, keeping token cost down in large casts.
GROUP_CHATS.P_GATING_2: Turn triggers on a character can force or suppress their participation based on message content; match whole words keeps short names from false-matching inside other words.
GROUP_CHATS.P_TIPS_1: Address characters by name to steer the scene. For a narrator character, keep always active on and give it low talkativeness so it speaks rarely but never loses context.

META.TITLE: CBS Macros in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: The curly-brace macro language: field tokens, seeded randomness, variables, calc, and block forms like if, each, and pure.
META.KEYWORDS: CBS macros, curly braced syntax, setvar getvar, random pick roll, macro blocks

MACROS.TITLE: Macros (CBS)
MACROS.SUBTITLE: Curly-brace scripting inside any prompt text.
MACROS.P_SYNTAX_1: Macros are double-brace tokens that expand at request time. They work in character fields, lorebook entries, presets, greetings, and plain chat text, and they nest.
MACROS.P_SYNTAX_2: Arguments are separated with double colons. Unknown macros expand to nothing rather than erroring, so a typo never breaks a request.
MACROS.M_CHAR: The current character's name (group chats: the current speaker).
MACROS.M_TIME: Current time / date in your locale and timezone.
MACROS.P_RANDOM_1: random picks one argument fresh each expansion, pick makes a choice that stays stable for the conversation, and roll throws dice with d-notation.
MACROS.P_RANDOM_2: Rolls and randoms are seeded per turn: a regenerate reuses the same values, so swiping does not reroll your dice.
MACROS.P_VARS_1: Chat variables persist per conversation branch; global variables persist across all chats. Set them in any macro-capable text or from trigger scripts.
MACROS.P_VARS_2: Branch-scoped storage means swiping to another branch restores that branch's variable state; siblings never leak values into each other.
MACROS.P_BLOCKS_1: Blocks wrap content: if renders its body only when the condition is truthy, each loops over arrays with slot substitution, and when adds line-based else branches.
MACROS.P_BLOCKS_2: pure and escape protect literal braces from expansion; any closing tag closes the innermost open block.
MACROS.P_COMMENTS_1: Comment macros vanish before the model ever sees them, which makes them ideal for notes inside card fields. Use pure blocks when you need to show macro syntax literally.

META.TITLE: Regex Scripts in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: Find-and-replace pipelines over input, output, prompt, and display text, with ordering and action meta directives.
META.KEYWORDS: regex scripts, customscript, editdisplay, editoutput, text transforms

REGEX_SCRIPTS.TITLE: Regex Scripts
REGEX_SCRIPTS.SUBTITLE: Automatic find-and-replace at four points in the pipeline.
REGEX_SCRIPTS.P_MODES_1: A regex script runs at one of four points:
REGEX_SCRIPTS.MODE_INPUT: Your message, before it enters the prompt.
REGEX_SCRIPTS.MODE_OUTPUT: The model's reply, before it is saved.
REGEX_SCRIPTS.MODE_DISPLAY: The rendered message; storage stays untouched.
REGEX_SCRIPTS.P_FIELDS_1: Each script is a pattern, a replacement (with $1-style capture references), and flags. Scripts attach to characters, so cards can ship their own text pipeline.
REGEX_SCRIPTS.P_FIELDS_2: editdisplay is the safe playground: it only changes what you see, never what is stored or sent, so a broken pattern cannot corrupt a chat.
REGEX_SCRIPTS.P_META_1: Directives inside the script body control execution: an order tag fixes the position in the pipeline when multiple scripts run in the same mode, and action directives move or transform the matched text instead of a plain replace.
REGEX_SCRIPTS.P_EXAMPLES_1: Convert asterisk emphasis into markup in the display layer:
REGEX_SCRIPTS.P_EXAMPLES_2: SillyTavern regex scripts import as part of character cards and run under the same modes.

META.TITLE: Trigger Scripts and Lua in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: Event-driven automation: the trigger VM, low-level effects, and the embedded Lua runtime with edit hooks.
META.KEYWORDS: trigger scripts, lua scripting, editoutput hook, roleplay automation

TRIGGERS_AND_LUA.TITLE: Triggers & Lua
TRIGGERS_AND_LUA.SUBTITLE: Automation that runs around every message.
TRIGGERS_AND_LUA.P_TRIGGERS_1: Triggers are event-driven scripts attached to characters. They fire at chat start or around messages, and can read history, set variables, inject system text, or stop a send.
TRIGGERS_AND_LUA.P_TRIGGERS_2: The script format uses indent-scoped commands compatible with RisuAI trigger scripts v2, so existing cards' automation imports and runs.
TRIGGERS_AND_LUA.P_EFFECTS_1: Scripts with low-level access unlock effects that reach outside the chat:
TRIGGERS_AND_LUA.P_EFFECTS_2: LLM and image effects call real models and cost tokens; they require being signed in and run through your account.
TRIGGERS_AND_LUA.P_LUA_1: For logic beyond the trigger VM, characters can carry Lua. The embedded runtime exposes an API of about 50 functions: chat access, variables, alerts, LLM calls, and more, compatible with RisuAI's Lua surface.
TRIGGERS_AND_LUA.P_HOOKS_1: Lua can register hooks that rewrite text in flight: your input before assembly, the model's output before saving, and the raw request right before it is sent.
TRIGGERS_AND_LUA.P_HOOKS_2: Hooks run in order with regex scripts of the same stage; use the request log to see the final result of the whole pipeline.
TRIGGERS_AND_LUA.P_SAFETY_1: Display and request script modes run in a sandbox with a restricted command set. Scripts cannot touch your account, keys, or other conversations; the worst a bad script can do is garble its own chat.

META.TITLE: Memory, Retrieval, and Web Search in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: Rolling story summaries, semantic retrieval of past moments, and classifier-gated web search.
META.KEYWORDS: chat memory, rolling summary, semantic retrieval, embeddings, web search

MEMORY_AND_CONTEXT.TITLE: Memory & Context
MEMORY_AND_CONTEXT.SUBTITLE: Keeping long stories coherent past the context window.
MEMORY_AND_CONTEXT.P_SUMMARY_1: With memory enabled, the oldest chunk of a long chat is folded into a running story-so-far summary and the summarized messages are cut from the prompt. The story keeps its shape while token use stays flat.
MEMORY_AND_CONTEXT.P_SUMMARY_2: Summarization runs on fast free models in the background; you keep chatting while it folds. The current summary rides along in a system block.
MEMORY_AND_CONTEXT.P_RETRIEVAL_1: Alongside the summary, recent chat is embedded and compared against older messages and lore candidates; the closest matches are injected as relevant background. Old details resurface exactly when the scene touches them.
MEMORY_AND_CONTEXT.P_WEBSEARCH_1: Per-conversation opt-in. A tiny classifier first decides whether your message actually needs fresh facts; only then does a real search run and its results join the context.
MEMORY_AND_CONTEXT.P_WEBSEARCH_2: Search engine and context size are configurable in the settings drawer. Web search is available on paid accounts.
MEMORY_AND_CONTEXT.P_SETTINGS_1: Memory and web search are per-conversation switches in the settings drawer; presets carry defaults for new chats. The utility model setting picks which model does the folding and background work.

META.TITLE: In-Chat Image Generation in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: Scene illustrations after replies: model choice, reference images, style templates, prompt preview, and inline media.
META.KEYWORDS: image generation, scene illustration, reference images, style template, inlay images

IMAGES.TITLE: Images
IMAGES.SUBTITLE: Illustrations generated from the scene, right in the chat.
IMAGES.P_ENABLE_1: Turn on image generation per conversation in the settings drawer, or set it as a preset default. Once enabled, replies can produce a scene illustration automatically.
IMAGES.P_FLOW_1: After a reply lands, a prompt-writer model reads it and writes an image prompt; the image model then renders it. The reply is never delayed: the image appears in place when ready.
IMAGES.P_FLOW_2: A placeholder marks the spot while generating; if generation fails, the chat simply continues without the image.
IMAGES.P_MODELS_1: Pick any catalog image model, or let the engine choose a free one. The prompt-writer uses your utility model. Custom-provider image models are dispatched directly to your own endpoint.
IMAGES.P_REFS_1: Upload reference images in the settings drawer to keep faces, outfits, or styles consistent across generations; the primary character's avatar can be included automatically.
IMAGES.P_REFS_2: Up to six references ride along per request, capped by what the image model accepts.
IMAGES.P_STYLES_1: Style templates prefill the prompt instruction with a look: photorealistic, anime, painterly, and more. Edit the instruction after applying a template to fine-tune your default look.
IMAGES.P_PREVIEW_1: With preview enabled, the written image prompt pauses for your review: edit it, approve it, or skip the image entirely.
IMAGES.P_PREVIEW_2: Any generated image can be regenerated in place from its overlay menu; the new render replaces the old one in the same spot.
IMAGES.P_INLAYS_2: tokens rendering from local storage. Exported conversations carry the bytes, so images survive the trip.

META.TITLE: Custom Providers in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: Bring your own OpenAI-compatible endpoint: model discovery, per-model tokenizers with HuggingFace support, and billing groups.
META.KEYWORDS: custom provider, bring your own key, openai compatible endpoint, custom tokenizer, huggingface tokenizer

CUSTOM_PROVIDERS.TITLE: Custom Providers
CUSTOM_PROVIDERS.SUBTITLE: Chat through your own endpoint and key.
CUSTOM_PROVIDERS.P_ADD_1: Add any OpenAI-compatible endpoint with a name, base URL, and API key. The provider and its key are stored only in your local database.
CUSTOM_PROVIDERS.P_ADD_2: Custom models appear in the model picker alongside catalog models; a conversation can switch between them freely.
CUSTOM_PROVIDERS.P_MODELS_1: Fetch the provider's model list automatically or add model ids by hand. Each model is typed as text or image; image-typed models feed the in-chat image generator instead of the chat dropdown.
CUSTOM_PROVIDERS.P_MODELS_2: Model entries carry their own settings, including the tokenizer used for budgeting.
CUSTOM_PROVIDERS.P_TOKENIZERS_1: Token counting drives history trimming and lorebook budgets, so the right tokenizer matters for long chats. Every custom model picks from 13 presets:
CUSTOM_PROVIDERS.P_TOKENIZERS_2: Or point at any HuggingFace tokenizer by slug or URL:
CUSTOM_PROVIDERS.P_TOKENIZERS_3: HuggingFace tokenizers download once and cache locally. Counting never blocks a send: if a tokenizer fails to load, an approximate fallback counts instead.
CUSTOM_PROVIDERS.P_GROUP_1: Catalog models can route through a billing group that seeds new chats. Custom-provider models bypass routing entirely, so the group has no effect on them.
CUSTOM_PROVIDERS.P_PRIVACY_1: Requests to custom providers go straight from your browser to your endpoint. {appName} servers never see the request, the reply, or your provider key.

META.TITLE: Data, Export, and Inspection in {appName}
META.DESCRIPTION: Conversation export formats, entity portability, the request log and dry-run inspectors, and the local database studio.
META.KEYWORDS: export chat, sillytavern jsonl, request log, dry run, local database, data portability

DATA.TITLE: Your Data
DATA.SUBTITLE: Everything is local; take it anywhere, inspect anything.
DATA.P_CONVERSATIONS_1: Export any conversation from the chat actions menu in three formats, and import the same formats back, including files from other apps:
DATA.X_NATIVE: Full-fidelity backup: branches, variables, media, and settings all survive.
DATA.X_ORPG: OpenRouter-compatible interchange with a lossless extension block.
DATA.X_ST: Moving chats to or from SillyTavern.
DATA.P_ENTITIES_1: Characters export as png, charx, voxta, or json; lorebooks as SillyTavern, Agnai, Risu, or CCv3 formats; presets and cards as JSON. Imports accept the same formats.
DATA.P_ENTITIES_2: Every entity list has one-click duplicate, which clones with a Copy suffix; lorebook duplicates deep-copy their entries.
DATA.P_INSPECT_1: The request log stores a debug snapshot per request: the assembled prompt, token counts, cost, and which parameters the provider dropped. Open it from the message menu.
DATA.P_INSPECT_2: Dry-run assembles the full prompt without calling the model, free of charge: the fastest way to check what a template, lorebook, or script actually produces.
DATA.P_DB_1: All chat data lives in a SQLite database in your browser's private storage, per account. The built-in DB studio can browse tables, download the whole database file, and import one back.
DATA.P_DB_2: Import reconciles into the current schema and re-maps ownership, so a backup from another account or an older version restores cleanly. Guests have the same local database; nothing requires an account.

QUICKSTART.TITLE: Quickstart

MODELS_AND_PRICING.TITLE: Models & Pricing
MODELS_AND_PRICING.SUBTITLE: What the :free suffix means, how usage is priced and why a model sometimes disappears.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_CATALOG_1: The Models page lists every model with context window, per-token prices, supported endpoints and capability filters like tool calling and image input. Each model has its own page with copy-paste code examples. Not every free model supports tool calls or vision, so check the capability badges before wiring one into a coding agent.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_CATALOG_2: Models rotate from provider to provider for stability, so the same model can show a slightly different price over time. Check the price on the model page if cost matters. Rankings shows which free models actually deliver, based on community test results, and Status tracks live provider health.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_DISCOUNTS_1: Every model has an availability rate and one or more providers behind it. Open a model's page and look at group pricing to see the per-provider prices it routes across.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_DISCOUNTS_2: Models with high availability and accessibility earn automatic discounts, often steep ones. When a provider stops working the model fails over to a more stable one, which can slightly change the discount.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_FREE_VS_PAID_1: Free models carry a :free suffix, for example
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_FREE_VS_PAID_2: A :free model routes only to free upstream providers and never touches your balance. The same base name without the suffix is the paid version: stable, uncapped and billed per token. Both can exist side by side, so switching from free to paid is a one-string change.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_FREE_VS_PAID_3: Free models are free for a reason: the upstream providers set the rate limits, not us. Expect 429 responses at peak times, and use a paid model when you need reliability.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_PRICING_1: Most models bill per token, with separate input and output prices. A few models (mostly image and video) bill a flat price per call instead. What you see on the model page is what you pay: no subscriptions, no hidden fees, your balance simply decreases per request.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_PRICING_2: The Pricing page has current top-up options; every model page shows live per-token prices.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_PROMPT_CACHE_1: For models that support prompt caching (Claude and others), repeated prompt prefixes are billed at a reduced cached-input rate, while writing a new cache entry costs slightly more than a normal input token (about 1.25x).
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_PROMPT_CACHE_2: Caching is automatic. Workloads with long stable system prompts (agents, RP presets) profit the most, with no configuration needed.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_AVAILABILITY_1: When a free model has several upstream providers, requests automatically fail over to the next one if a provider hits its rate limit. Single-provider models cannot fail over, so they stall until the limit resets.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_AVAILABILITY_2: Each model runs across one or more provider channels. A channel that hits its rate limit is temporarily disabled and hidden, it is not shown as an option while it recovers. As long as one channel is still up, the model keeps working through it. Only when every channel for a model is rate limited does the model itself disappear from the catalog.
MODELS_AND_PRICING.P_AVAILABILITY_3: A model vanishing from the list is expected under load, not a typo or an outage. It reappears on its own once a channel passes a health check, usually within minutes. If a saved model name stops resolving, check the Models page: it is either recovering or has been renamed.

META.TITLE: Provider group pinning
META.DESCRIPTION: Pin models on an API key to specific provider groups: lock billing to their rates, route cheapest-first among them, and fail over automatically.
